    Derived sequence

    The Snake Lemma, as a document

    Setting. A commutative diagram of abelian groups (or modules) with exact rows:

    The Snake Lemma. There is a connecting map δ making this sequence exact:

    ker α → ker β → ker γ —δ→ coker α → coker β → coker γ

    Constructing δ in six moves

    1. Start in the kernel. Take c′ ∈ C′ with γ(c′) = 0.
    2. Lift left (a choice). p′ is surjective, so choose b′ ∈ B′ with p′(b′) = c′.
    3. Move down. Apply β to get β(b′) ∈ B.
    4. Discover a kernel condition. p(β(b′)) = γ(p′(b′)) = γ(c′) = 0 because the right square commutes; so β(b′) ∈ ker p.
    5. Move left by exactness. ker p = im i, so i(a) = β(b′) for some a ∈ A, unique because i is injective.
    6. Pass to the quotient. Define δ(c′) = [a] ∈ A / im α = coker α.

    Why δ is well defined

    If b′₁ and b′₂ both lift c′, then p′(b′₁ − b′₂) = 0, so b′₁ − b′₂ ∈ ker p′ = im i′: b′₁ − b′₂ = i′(a′). Then β(b′₁) − β(b′₂) = β(i′(a′)) = i(α(a′)), and since i is injective, a₁ − a₂ = α(a′). Hence [a₁] = [a₂] in coker α: different lifts differ by exactly the information the cokernel kills. The same argument shows δ is a homomorphism.

    Exactness, briefly

    • At ker β: if b′ ∈ ker β and p′(b′) = 0 then b′ = i′(a′); i(α(a′)) = β(b′) = 0, so α(a′) = 0 and a′ ∈ ker α.
    • At ker γ: if δ(c′) = [a] = 0 then a = α(a′); the corrected lift b′ − i′(a′) lies in ker β and still maps to c′.
    • At coker α: if [i(a)] = 0 in coker β then i(a) = β(b′); γ(p′(b′)) = p(i(a)) = 0, and δ(p′(b′)) = [a].
    • At coker β: if p(b) = γ(c′), lift c′ = p′(b′); p(b − β(b′)) = 0 so b − β(b′) = i(a) and [b] = [i(a)].

    A concrete example over ℤ

    Both rows are 0 → ℤ → ℤ² → ℤ → 0 with i(a) = (a, 0) and p(a, c) = c. Take α(a) = 2a, γ(c) = 0 and β(a, c) = (2a + c, 0); both squares commute. Then ker γ = ℤ and coker α = ℤ/2ℤ. Starting from c′ = 1 with lift b′ = (k, 1): β(k, 1) = (2k + 1, 0), so a = 2k + 1 and δ(1) = [2k + 1] = [1] for every k. In general δ(n) = n mod 2.

    A note on elements

    The Snake Lemma is valid in any abelian category. The moving-element visualisation models the familiar proof in modules/abelian groups; it should not imply that arbitrary abelian categories literally have elements.
